title: Testing an ML Spacecraft Anomaly Detector Beyond Accuracy
description: Why accuracy, precision and F1 are not enough for a spacecraft anomaly detector — and which tests reveal drift, unseen anomalies, sensor dropouts and latency risks.
author: Embedded AI & ML Verification Engineer (portfolio author)
seoTitle: Testing a Spacecraft Anomaly Detector Beyond Accuracy — Engineering Note
seoDescription: Operational testing of ML anomaly detection: unseen anomalies, drift, sensor dropout, latency and fallback.

content.text: Accuracy is meaningless on strongly imbalanced telemetry: a detector that always says 'nominal' can still score 97%. Accuracy, precision and recall summarize a single operating point on one dataset; they say nothing about drift, novel anomalies or degraded sensors.
False positives drain operator attention and can trigger unnecessary FDIR reactions. The acceptance criterion must be an explicit false-positive budget per unit of time.
A missed anomaly can propagate through the platform undetected. False negatives are the reason anomaly detectors need fallback, ground review and drift monitoring rather than silent autonomy.
A detector that flags an anomaly ten minutes late may be operationally useless. Measure detection delay in windows, not only binary recall.
Random splits on ordered telemetry leak future samples into training. Split chronologically or by campaign so verification measures generalization forward in time.

Hold out whole anomaly families, not just random rows. In the Telemetry Anomaly Detector, known-anomaly recall reached 0.97 while an unseen family dropped to 0.61 — a difference no single score would reveal.
Verify behaviour when an entire channel disappears, including whether the detector flags the condition explicitly.
Test missing-sample rates inside the declared tolerance and confirm graceful, bounded degradation.
Inject expected sensor noise and confirm recall and false-positive behaviour remain inside budget.

Slow sensor ageing changes input distributions. In the TAD campaign, drift was flagged only after 38% of the run and FPR grew to 3.1× nominal — a FAIL against the requirement, and the reason drift threshold tuning is an open mitigation.
A mode change or new software version can shift telemetry instantly. Test abrupt shifts separately from gradual ramps.
Out-of-distribution inputs must be detected or conservatively flagged, never scored silently with full confidence.
High-rate bursts stress detection cadence and logging. Confirm a bounded fraction of burst events is caught.
An anomaly flag that arrives after the FDIR window is worthless. Measure p95 latency on the target, plus CPU and memory headroom — not only on the development host.
Every flag, score, latency sample and drift indicator must be logged with the input context needed for later review.
Document how thresholds are chosen and which operating point they produce. Thresholds are parameters of the deployed system, not of the model card only.
Monitor false-alarm trends, anomaly-rate drift, sensor distribution drift and the missed-anomaly review queue.
Define what happens on low confidence or OOD: deterministic threshold checks, ground-analysis request, or safe state.
After testing, the residual risk is explicit: for TAD, rare unseen anomalies remain the main accepted-with-limitations risk, with drift monitoring as a condition.

This campaign uses synthetic telemetry in a simulated environment; it does not validate behaviour on a real spacecraft or flight computer. Target latency could not be measured (environment unavailable). Drift and unseen-anomaly results reflect the demonstration datasets and should not be extrapolated to other platforms without new data.

items: Baseline FP budget defined per time unit
OOD inputs detected, not silently scored

content.text: Verification of an anomaly detector is operational, not statistical. The tests that matter are the ones that simulate how the system will be used and misused: drift, dropouts, novel patterns and deadlines.
